groups.title: Boot and Spring
groups.mechanism: Boot assembles an opinionated Spring application through dependency management, conditional configuration and operational integrations. It does not replace Spring's underlying container or transaction semantics.
groups.tradeOff: Conventions reduce setup but defaults must fit the deployed application.
groups.verify: Compare the resolved dependencies and registered beans of a minimal application.

questions.question: What problem does Spring Boot solve?
questions.answer: It reduces repetitive Spring application setup through starters, managed dependency versions, conditional auto-configuration and executable packaging.

questions.question: When should Boot conventions be overridden?
questions.answer: When a measured requirement or explicit contract differs from the default. Override the narrowest supported setting and verify the resulting behavior.

questions.question: How does Boot depend on Spring Framework?
questions.answer: Boot configures and integrates Spring components; DI, MVC and transaction contracts remain those of the selected Spring Framework version.

questions.question: Why is adding a starter not proof a feature is configured correctly?
questions.answer: Conditions, missing properties and custom beans can change activation. Verify actual wiring and behavior rather than classpath presence alone.

questions.question: How would you evaluate a Boot upgrade?
questions.answer: Inspect the release and dependency changes, preserve API and data contracts, run representative integration tests and rehearse rollback compatibility.

groups.title: Application startup
groups.mechanism: SpringApplication prepares the environment and context before starting the application. Startup completion and business readiness are separate operational decisions.
groups.tradeOff: Failing early improves safety, while optional dependency checks should not cause unnecessary restart loops.
groups.verify: Start with missing required settings and with an unavailable optional integration.

questions.question: What does SpringApplication.run do?
questions.answer: It bootstraps a Spring application context and coordinates startup using the application's configuration and environment.

questions.question: When should ApplicationRunner be used?
questions.answer: For bounded startup work requiring the initialized context, while defining whether failure should prevent readiness or abort startup.

questions.question: How do runners affect startup completion?
questions.answer: Configured runners execute during application startup before the application is considered fully ready by the normal startup sequence.

questions.question: Why is an unbounded warm-up loop in a runner dangerous?
questions.answer: It can block startup indefinitely and retain resources, causing repeated failed deployments without a useful readiness signal.

questions.question: How would you make startup work recoverable?
questions.answer: Use bounded retries and durable progress for essential work; keep idempotency and ownership explicit across application restarts.

groups.title: Auto-configuration conditions
groups.mechanism: Auto-configuration imports candidate configurations and evaluates conditions involving classes, properties and beans. A user definition can cause selected defaults to back off.
groups.tradeOff: Convenient conditional wiring can surprise users when dependencies change.
groups.verify: Inspect a conditions report before and after adding a custom bean.

questions.question: What is auto-configuration?
questions.answer: Boot's conditional registration of useful configuration based on the application's classpath, environment and existing bean definitions.

questions.question: When does a custom bean replace a Boot default?
questions.answer: When the relevant auto-configuration condition is designed to back off for that bean type or name; verify the specific configuration contract.

questions.question: How are auto-configuration candidates registered in modern Boot?
questions.answer: Through the supported auto-configuration imports mechanism, rather than relying on arbitrary component scanning of library packages.

questions.question: Why can a dependency addition change application behavior unexpectedly?
questions.answer: New classes can satisfy conditions and activate configuration that previously did not apply, changing beans or operational endpoints.

questions.question: How would you debug an unexpected DataSource bean?
questions.answer: Inspect condition outcomes, effective properties and user definitions, then trace the dependency that supplied the relevant auto-configuration classes.

groups.title: Starters and BOMs
groups.mechanism: Starters describe useful dependency sets; a BOM manages compatible versions without automatically adding every dependency. Resolved graphs determine the actual runtime.
groups.tradeOff: Central management improves compatibility while independent overrides can create binary conflicts.
groups.verify: Inspect the dependency tree and effective build after any override.

questions.question: What is a Boot starter?
questions.answer: A curated dependency entry point for a common application capability, reducing manual coordination of related libraries.

questions.question: What is the difference between dependency management and a dependency?
questions.answer: Management supplies defaults such as versions; an actual dependency declaration places an artifact on the relevant graph.

questions.question: How does a Boot BOM help compatibility?
questions.answer: It aligns many library versions tested as a platform, reducing accidental mismatches between independently selected components.

questions.question: Why can overriding one transitive version break startup?
questions.answer: Other components may expect different binary APIs, leading to linkage errors even when the application source compiles.

questions.question: How would you address a vulnerable managed dependency?
questions.answer: Inspect the introducing path and supported platform updates first; validate any necessary override against the full resolved graph and runtime tests.

groups.title: External configuration
groups.mechanism: Boot combines packaged and external sources according to defined precedence. Binding, validation and activation remain separate steps.
groups.tradeOff: External flexibility requires documented ownership and safe exposure of effective settings.
groups.verify: Test conflicting sources, missing secrets and invalid typed values.

questions.question: Why externalize application configuration?
questions.answer: To deploy one artifact with environment-specific settings while keeping required invariants explicit and validated.

questions.question: When are grouped configuration properties preferable to Value strings?
questions.answer: For related settings with shared types, defaults and cross-field validation, reducing scattered independent lookups.

questions.question: What is configuration precedence?
questions.answer: The rule deciding which property source wins when the same key appears in several supported locations.

questions.question: Why can an environment variable override a packaged value unexpectedly?
questions.answer: External sources can have higher precedence. Inspect the effective binding and deployment inputs rather than reading only application.properties.

questions.question: How would you expose configuration diagnostics safely?
questions.answer: Publish permitted effective modes and origins, redact secrets, restrict management access and test that sensitive values never appear in responses or logs.

groups.title: Typed configuration validation
groups.mechanism: ConfigurationProperties binds settings into a model. Validation must reject unusable combinations, not merely values that parse.
groups.tradeOff: Safe defaults simplify setup but must not disguise missing production requirements.
groups.verify: Exercise blank endpoints, invalid durations and contradictory enabled flags.

questions.question: What does ConfigurationProperties provide?
questions.answer: Structured binding of related external settings into a typed object with a stable prefix and optional validation.

questions.question: When should a configuration default be rejected?
questions.answer: When silently using it would violate production safety or business behavior, such as sending real traffic to a sandbox endpoint.

questions.question: How is parsing different from validating configuration?
questions.answer: A URI or duration can parse successfully while still violating allowed schemes, destinations or operational bounds.

questions.question: Why is NotNull insufficient for an endpoint?
questions.answer: A non-null URI can still be relative, use an unsupported scheme or target an unapproved host; validate the intended contract.

questions.question: How would you update related settings atomically?
questions.answer: Treat them as one validated configuration version and define replacement plus in-flight behavior; ordinary binding does not promise automatic live refresh.

groups.title: Profiles and deployment modes
groups.mechanism: Profiles select configuration and beans. Multiple active profiles can combine, so deployment modes need explicit valid combinations.
groups.tradeOff: Profile-based convenience becomes difficult when used as an unbounded feature system.
groups.verify: Start every supported profile combination and assert selected integrations.

questions.question: What is a Boot profile used for?
questions.answer: Selecting environment-specific properties and Spring bean composition through the application's supported profile mechanism.

questions.question: When should a feature flag replace a profile?
questions.answer: When a runtime business capability needs independent targeting or change policy rather than a broad application composition mode.

questions.question: How can profile-specific configuration interact with external sources?
questions.answer: Both activation and precedence affect the final values; the presence of a profile file does not make it the winning source.

questions.question: Why can enabling test and production profiles together be dangerous?
questions.answer: Conflicting fake and real integrations may become eligible simultaneously, producing ambiguous wiring or unsafe fallbacks.

questions.question: How would you prevent accidental sandbox activation in production?
questions.answer: Validate deployment mode centrally, restrict fake beans to explicit conditions and assert the actual selected client before accepting traffic.

groups.title: HTTP server choices
groups.mechanism: Boot supports different web stacks and embedded-server integrations. MVC and WebFlux have different execution and testing models.
groups.tradeOff: A familiar programming model may be simpler than switching stacks for unmeasured throughput claims.
groups.verify: Identify the actual server and exercise blocking dependencies under load.

questions.question: What is an embedded server in Boot?
questions.answer: A server integration started as part of the application's executable process rather than requiring a separately deployed application server.

questions.question: When should MVC be preferred to WebFlux?
questions.answer: When a synchronous stack fits the dependencies and team; assess streaming and concurrency needs instead of choosing by assumed performance superiority.

questions.question: How does Boot choose web application behavior?
questions.answer: From configured application type and available dependencies under supported auto-configuration rules; verify the selected stack in the actual build.

questions.question: Why can adding both web starters produce a surprising result?
questions.answer: Classpath-based selection follows Boot's rules rather than the developer's naming intention; explicitly verify which stack is active.

questions.question: How would you diagnose slow HTTP handling after changing servers?
questions.answer: Compare queueing, worker limits, connection behavior and dependency latency with equivalent endpoints and workload.

groups.title: Actuator endpoints
groups.mechanism: Actuator exposes operational information through configured management interfaces. Endpoint availability, exposure and authorization are separate concerns.
groups.tradeOff: Operational visibility is useful but can disclose sensitive internals or enable powerful actions.
groups.verify: Test management access from both permitted and untrusted network paths.

questions.question: What does Actuator add?
questions.answer: Production-oriented management capabilities such as health information and integration with metrics and application diagnostics.

questions.question: When should management traffic use a separate interface or port?
questions.answer: When network isolation and access policy benefit from separation; verify routing, authentication and monitoring reachability explicitly.

questions.question: Does enabling an endpoint automatically make it publicly accessible?
questions.answer: No. Availability, exposure and security configuration jointly determine reachability, and those rules vary by endpoint and version.

questions.question: Why is broad management exposure risky?
questions.answer: Diagnostic data and administrative operations can reveal internal structure or permit unintended control if insufficiently restricted.

questions.question: How would you validate an Actuator security policy?
questions.answer: Enumerate exposed endpoints and test anonymous, authenticated and authorized access, including alternate management paths and error responses.

groups.title: Health and readiness
groups.mechanism: Liveness, readiness and startup checks answer different questions. Dependency health should reflect whether the instance can usefully serve its promised capability.
groups.tradeOff: Aggressive checks can amplify outages by removing all instances or repeatedly restarting them.
groups.verify: Simulate a slow dependency and inspect routing plus restart behavior.

questions.question: How do liveness and readiness differ?
questions.answer: Liveness asks whether restart may recover a broken process; readiness asks whether the instance should currently receive traffic.

questions.question: When should a dependency affect readiness?
questions.answer: When its failure prevents the instance from providing required service, according to an explicit degradation and routing policy.

questions.question: Why is a successful health endpoint insufficient for a business SLO?
questions.answer: It may exercise a cheaper path than user requests and omit overloaded pools, stale data or failing dependencies.

questions.question: How can dependency-based liveness cause an outage loop?
questions.answer: A shared external failure can trigger restarts across healthy processes without repairing the dependency, adding cold-start load.

questions.question: How would you test probe behavior during deployment?
questions.answer: Introduce slow startup and dependency failure, then verify traffic admission, graceful withdrawal and bounded restart behavior.

groups.title: Metrics and tracing
groups.mechanism: Boot integrates observation infrastructure, but useful telemetry still requires stable naming, bounded labels and meaningful boundaries.
groups.tradeOff: Detailed dimensions aid diagnosis while unbounded cardinality can overwhelm monitoring systems.
groups.verify: Check a successful request, retry, timeout and asynchronous handoff end to end.

questions.question: What is the purpose of application metrics?
questions.answer: To quantify throughput, errors, latency and resource pressure over time using measurements aligned with operational questions.

questions.question: When should a request identifier be logged rather than used as a metric tag?
questions.answer: When its cardinality is effectively unbounded. Logs or traces can carry individual identities without creating one time series per request.

questions.question: How do retries affect latency observations?
questions.answer: A measurement around the entire operation differs from one around each attempt. Define both boundaries when diagnosing retry overhead.

questions.question: Why can tracing disappear after an executor handoff?
questions.answer: Context may not propagate through arbitrary task submission. Use supported propagation and verify both success and failure paths.

questions.question: How would you detect a connection-pool bottleneck?
questions.answer: Correlate acquisition wait, active connections, query latency and request deadlines instead of relying only on HTTP duration metrics.

groups.title: Boot testing layers
groups.mechanism: Boot test support can load focused slices or broad application contexts. Selecting the boundary matters more than maximizing context size.
groups.tradeOff: Narrow slices run quickly but omit integrations; full contexts can hide expensive or accidental coupling.
groups.verify: Verify representative behavior with the smallest test that includes the relevant real boundary.

questions.question: What is SpringBootTest intended for?
questions.answer: Bootstrapping application-level integration tests using Boot configuration, with web environment chosen explicitly by the test.

questions.question: When is a web slice test useful?
questions.answer: For controller routing, binding, validation and HTTP behavior while controlling collaborators and acknowledging excluded infrastructure.

questions.question: How does a repository slice differ from a real production database test?
questions.answer: Its database, dialect and selected configuration may differ, so it cannot establish every production SQL, locking or migration behavior.

questions.question: Why can a transactional HTTP integration test leave rows behind?
questions.answer: The server request can execute on another thread and transaction, outside the test thread's rollback scope.

questions.question: How would you balance the Boot test suite?
questions.answer: Use unit tests for decisions, slices for framework boundaries and a smaller set of real packaged/infrastructure tests for integration risks.

groups.title: Database integration
groups.mechanism: Boot can configure data sources and persistence support, while transaction and database semantics remain explicit application concerns.
groups.tradeOff: Convenient setup does not make pool size, migration ownership or query behavior universally correct.
groups.verify: Start with schema drift, pool exhaustion and a rollback scenario.

questions.question: What does data-source auto-configuration do?
questions.answer: It can assemble supported connection infrastructure from dependencies and settings when its conditions apply.

questions.question: When should pool size be changed?
questions.answer: After observing connection waits and database capacity. More connections can increase contention and memory without improving throughput.

questions.question: How do schema migration tools fit startup?
questions.answer: They apply versioned database changes under configured lifecycle rules; application and deployment ownership must prevent conflicting migration execution.

questions.question: Why is automatic schema mutation risky for production?
questions.answer: Unexpected changes can alter or destroy data without a reviewed migration and rollback-compatible rollout plan.

questions.question: How would you roll out a new required column?
questions.answer: Use expand-contract steps: add compatible schema, deploy tolerant readers and writers, backfill safely, then enforce stricter constraints when all consumers permit it.

groups.title: Security integration
groups.mechanism: Boot supplies conditional defaults and integrations; application-specific authorization still requires explicit policy. Authentication does not establish ownership of a requested resource.
groups.tradeOff: Defaults help safe startup but are not a complete product security model.
groups.verify: Test anonymous, wrong-role and wrong-tenant requests plus management endpoints.

questions.question: Does adding the security starter complete API security?
questions.answer: No. Define identity trust, route policy, object-level authorization, session or token behavior and operational endpoint access.

questions.question: When should resource-server support be used?
questions.answer: When validating bearer tokens under a configured trusted issuer and required claims, rather than implementing ad hoc token parsing.

questions.question: How do authentication and authorization differ?
questions.answer: Authentication establishes a trusted identity; authorization determines whether that identity may perform a specific action on a specific resource.

questions.question: Why can a valid token still be rejected correctly?
questions.answer: It may have the wrong audience, insufficient permission, wrong tenant or invalid time claims for the operation.

questions.question: How would you verify a custom security configuration after an upgrade?
questions.answer: Replay positive and negative route cases, validate token trust and claim rules, and check filter ordering plus management exposure.

groups.title: Packaging and containers
groups.mechanism: Executable packaging assembles application code and dependencies into a deployable artifact. Container layers and buildpacks affect rebuild cost and runtime environment.
groups.tradeOff: A smaller image is useful only if security, diagnostics and compatibility remain adequate.
groups.verify: Run the produced artifact in the target container rather than only through the IDE.

questions.question: What is an executable Boot JAR?
questions.answer: A packaged application with launcher support and dependencies arranged so the application can run as an executable Java artifact.

questions.question: When are layered images useful?
questions.answer: When separating changing application code from more stable dependencies improves image reuse, build speed and deployment transfer cost.

questions.question: What is a buildpack-based image build?
questions.answer: A supported process that turns application artifacts into an OCI image using builder-provided build and runtime conventions.

questions.question: Why can a container pass local startup but fail in deployment?
questions.answer: Architecture, certificates, filesystem permissions, memory limits or environment inputs can differ from the developer machine.

questions.question: How would you harden a production application image?
questions.answer: Use a supported minimal runtime, non-root execution where possible, controlled writable paths and verified dependencies while preserving required diagnostics.

groups.title: Graceful shutdown
groups.mechanism: Shutdown must coordinate traffic withdrawal, accepted work and resource cleanup under a finite deployment deadline.
groups.tradeOff: Long drain windows preserve more work but delay rollout and still cannot guarantee forced-kill cleanup.
groups.verify: Terminate the process during short, long and side-effecting requests.

questions.question: What is graceful shutdown trying to achieve?
questions.answer: Stopping new work while allowing accepted operations to finish within a bounded period before resources and the process terminate.

questions.question: When should readiness change during termination?
questions.answer: Early enough for routing to stop sending new work, while allowing for propagation delay and existing connections.

questions.question: How does a shutdown timeout affect long-running requests?
questions.answer: Work beyond the allowed drain period may be interrupted or disconnected; the client-visible outcome can remain uncertain after a side effect.

questions.question: Why are shutdown hooks insufficient for durable business recovery?
questions.answer: Abrupt termination can skip hooks. Persist enough state to reconcile or resume unfinished work after restart.

questions.question: How would you validate a rolling update's termination policy?
questions.answer: Measure routing withdrawal, in-flight completion, resource closure and recovery of ambiguous operations under the actual orchestrator timing.

groups.title: AOT and native images
groups.mechanism: Spring AOT processes application configuration for optimized execution; GraalVM native-image compilation is a separate step with closed-world constraints.
groups.tradeOff: Startup and footprint benefits compete with build cost, library compatibility and diagnostic differences.
groups.verify: Exercise the actual native artifact with deployment-specific configuration and rare code paths.

questions.question: Does Spring Boot support native images?
questions.answer: Yes, through supported Spring AOT and GraalVM native-image integration, subject to version and dependency compatibility.

questions.question: When does native packaging deserve a prototype?
questions.answer: When measured startup or memory constraints dominate, and the service's libraries and operational tooling can support the target.

questions.question: What are runtime hints used for?
questions.answer: To describe dynamic access and resources needed by AOT or native processing when they cannot be discovered adequately through ordinary analysis.

questions.question: Why is a passing JVM test insufficient for a native release?
questions.answer: Reachability, resource inclusion, initialization and dynamic behavior differ in the native artifact.

questions.question: How would you compare JVM and native deployments fairly?
questions.answer: Use equivalent behavior, traffic, resource limits and dependencies; compare readiness, footprint, steady throughput, tail latency and build/diagnostic costs.

groups.title: Dependency upgrades and compatibility
groups.mechanism: The platform version aligns a matrix of framework, library and plugin behavior. Major upgrades can alter namespaces, APIs and defaults.
groups.tradeOff: Staying current reduces maintenance risk but upgrades must preserve observable contracts.
groups.verify: Inspect resolved graphs and test old requests, persisted states and rollback compatibility.

questions.question: Why should Boot and Spring versions normally be aligned?
questions.answer: Boot's dependency management defines a supported combination; arbitrary framework overrides can produce untested binary and behavioral interactions.

questions.question: When is a major Boot upgrade more than a version edit?
questions.answer: When it changes Java requirements, namespaces, framework contracts, configuration properties or supported dependencies.

questions.question: How would you find deprecated configuration before upgrading?
questions.answer: Use release guidance, configuration metadata and relevant migration tooling, then verify effective behavior in the upgraded application.

questions.question: Why can a successful compile conceal an upgrade regression?
questions.answer: Serialization, security defaults, queries, management exposure and runtime wiring can change without a compiler error.

questions.question: How would you stage a major framework migration?
questions.answer: Inventory contracts, update compatible infrastructure first, test representative flows, canary with stop thresholds and preserve a viable data-compatible rollback.

groups.title: Production diagnosis
groups.mechanism: Operational incidents need an evidence-based decomposition of startup, traffic, dependencies and resource limits. Boot diagnostics are tools rather than conclusions.
groups.tradeOff: Collecting everything indiscriminately can add overhead and expose sensitive data.
groups.verify: Reproduce one controlled failure and trace it through logs, metrics and dependency timing.

questions.question: Where should a Boot startup failure investigation begin?
questions.answer: With the earliest causal exception, condition outcomes, effective required settings and the actual packaged dependency graph.

questions.question: When is the conditions report more useful than changing annotations?
questions.answer: When a bean is unexpectedly present or absent because auto-configuration conditions did not match the developer's assumption.

questions.question: How do you separate CPU saturation from downstream waiting?
questions.answer: Compare CPU profiles, thread state, connection acquisition and distributed traces alongside latency and throughput.

questions.question: Why can a healthy instance produce many timeouts?
questions.answer: Readiness can omit saturated queues or dependencies, and requests may spend most of their deadline waiting before execution.

questions.question: How would you close an incident investigation with evidence?
questions.answer: Reproduce the cause, apply the smallest corrective change, run a representative load/failure test and record residual limitations plus rollback steps.

groups.title: Custom auto-configuration
groups.mechanism: Reusable Boot modules should declare explicit conditions, defaults and extension points. User overrides and ordering must be verified rather than assumed.
groups.tradeOff: Opinionated defaults are helpful only when back-off behavior remains predictable.
groups.verify: Test the module with missing classes, custom user beans and invalid properties.

questions.question: When should a reusable integration supply auto-configuration?
questions.answer: When several applications need consistent conditional setup with documented defaults and clear user override behavior.

questions.question: What should an auto-configuration module expose as its contract?
questions.answer: Required dependencies, property names, conditions, produced bean types, lifecycle, security expectations and supported override points.

questions.question: How can ApplicationContextRunner support auto-configuration tests?
questions.answer: It creates controlled contexts with selected configuration and inputs, making activation and back-off behavior practical to assert.

questions.question: Why should auto-configuration avoid broad component scans?
questions.answer: Broad scanning can register unrelated components and make library behavior depend on package contents rather than explicit configuration.

questions.question: How would you prevent a library upgrade from changing application wiring silently?
questions.answer: Test activation matrices and user overrides across supported platform versions, inspect bean identities and document intentional behavior changes.

groups.title: @SpringBootApplication composition
groups.mechanism: SpringBootApplication composes Boot configuration, auto-configuration enablement and component scanning. Each part is handled by its own configuration infrastructure, not one magical startup action.
groups.tradeOff: Convention reduces setup while package placement and conditional activation remain consequential.
groups.verify: Move a component outside the scan root and inspect the resulting definitions plus condition report.

questions.question: Which annotations does @SpringBootApplication compose?
questions.answer: It combines SpringBootConfiguration, EnableAutoConfiguration and ComponentScan, bringing related but distinct configuration mechanisms together.

questions.question: Why does the application class's package matter?
questions.answer: Its default scan location influences discovered application components; deliberate package boundaries avoid missing or accidentally registered beans.

questions.question: Does scanBasePackages control every persistence scan?
questions.answer: No. Component scanning, entity discovery and repository scanning have separate configuration contracts and must be verified independently.

questions.question: Why can an application start while a controller is absent?
questions.answer: Its component was not discovered or eligible, so startup can succeed without registering the intended route.

questions.question: How would you diagnose a startup-annotation misunderstanding?
questions.answer: Separate component discovery, auto-configuration imports and persistence scanning, then inspect the actual definitions and routes produced by each.

groups.title: @EnableAutoConfiguration and @AutoConfiguration
groups.mechanism: EnableAutoConfiguration imports candidate configuration through Boot infrastructure. AutoConfiguration marks library configuration for that mechanism; conditional metadata decides activation.
groups.tradeOff: Automatic integration depends on stable imports and deliberate back-off, not broad package scans.
groups.verify: Test a library with and without its optional classes and with an application-provided replacement bean.

questions.question: How does @EnableAutoConfiguration work internally?
questions.answer: It activates Boot's import-selection infrastructure, loading registered candidates and applying exclusion plus condition logic before configuration is used.

questions.question: What does @AutoConfiguration indicate?
questions.answer: A configuration intended for Boot's auto-configuration mechanism, with supported ordering metadata and conditional registration behavior.

questions.question: Why use AutoConfiguration.imports for library registration?
questions.answer: It explicitly identifies supported auto-configuration candidates through the modern Boot mechanism rather than relying on consumer scans.

questions.question: Does auto-configuration ordering determine ordinary bean initialization order?
questions.answer: Not universally. Configuration ordering and dependency-driven bean construction are different concerns; declare actual dependencies explicitly.

questions.question: How would you test custom auto-configuration back-off?
questions.answer: Create controlled contexts with missing prerequisites and user-defined beans, then assert selected identities, counts and lifecycle behavior.

groups.title: @ConditionalOnClass and @ConditionalOnMissingBean
groups.mechanism: Boot condition implementations evaluate metadata and bean availability at defined phases. Matching depends on what has been processed and the exact type search contract.
groups.tradeOff: Conditional defaults support extensibility while hidden return types or ordering assumptions can break intended overrides.
groups.verify: Vary classpath and user definitions and inspect condition outcomes rather than annotations alone.

questions.question: What does @ConditionalOnClass check?
questions.answer: Whether specified classes are available under the supported condition-processing rules; it does not establish correct configuration or external-system availability.

questions.question: How does @ConditionalOnMissingBean support overrides?
questions.answer: It allows selected defaults to register only when matching beans are absent under its configured search and type rules.

questions.question: Why should a @Bean return type expose useful concrete type information?
questions.answer: Condition evaluation and type prediction rely on available metadata; overly general return types can hide types needed by later conditions.

questions.question: Why can a missing-bean condition behave unexpectedly in user configuration?
questions.answer: Its evaluation sees definitions processed at that point, so unsupported ordering assumptions can change what is considered present.

questions.question: How would you debug duplicate conditional clients?
questions.answer: Inspect candidate types, factory return metadata, context search scope and configuration ordering, then make the intended override contract explicit.

groups.title: @ConditionalOnProperty and configuration modes
groups.mechanism: Property conditions gate registration; typed configuration binding and validation happen through separate mechanisms. A present property can still contain an invalid business value.
groups.tradeOff: Compact switches are useful but defaults and match-if-missing behavior need careful review.
groups.verify: Test absent, blank, false, true and unexpected values with the configured condition attributes.

questions.question: What does @ConditionalOnProperty control?
questions.answer: Whether configuration or a bean is eligible based on selected environment properties and its declared matching rules.

questions.question: Does @ConditionalOnProperty validate a whole settings object?
questions.answer: No. It evaluates its property condition; type conversion, endpoint safety and cross-field rules need binding and validation.

questions.question: Why should havingValue and matchIfMissing be explicit when important?
questions.answer: They clarify which values and absent settings activate behavior instead of leaving critical modes dependent on implicit defaults.

questions.question: Why can a false-valued property still be mishandled by application logic?
questions.answer: Independent code may interpret presence rather than the condition's semantics, creating divergent enabled/disabled decisions.

questions.question: How would you design a safe optional integration?
questions.answer: Use one typed enabled mode, validate required fields when enabled and ensure missing production configuration cannot activate a fake fallback.

groups.title: @ConfigurationProperties registration and validation
groups.mechanism: ConfigurationProperties describes binding metadata; EnableConfigurationProperties or ConfigurationPropertiesScan can register supported binding targets. Validation requires the relevant validation integration and constraints.
groups.tradeOff: Typed settings improve contracts while immutable construction and version differences require explicit tests.
groups.verify: Bind valid, missing, malformed and cross-field invalid values through the actual application context.

questions.question: Does @ConfigurationProperties alone always register a bean?
questions.answer: No universal registration follows from the annotation alone; use the supported registration mechanism or an intentional managed bean definition.

questions.question: How do @EnableConfigurationProperties and @ConfigurationPropertiesScan differ?
questions.answer: One explicitly lists binding types; the other discovers eligible configuration-properties types under its scan rules.

questions.question: What does @Validated add to a properties type?
questions.answer: It requests supported validation during binding, with an installed validation provider and applicable constraints.

questions.question: Why can valid-looking properties still fail startup?
questions.answer: Conversion or constructor invariants can fail, nested validation can reject values, or required combinations can be inconsistent.

questions.question: How would you test immutable configuration binding?
questions.answer: Load the actual binding target with representative source precedence and invalid combinations, then assert the constructed values or explicit startup rejection.

groups.title: @SpringBootTest and slice annotation internals
groups.mechanism: Boot test annotations integrate bootstrap, context selection and test customizers. Slice annotations restrict configuration and auto-configuration rather than promising a full production deployment.
groups.tradeOff: Focused contexts improve feedback but can omit the boundary whose behavior matters.
groups.verify: Inspect loaded beans and exercise a real failure relevant to each chosen test scope.

questions.question: How does @SpringBootTest locate application configuration?
questions.answer: Boot test bootstrap support searches or uses declared configuration according to its supported rules, then creates the selected application context and web environment.

questions.question: What does @WebMvcTest intentionally narrow?
questions.answer: It focuses on MVC-related components and test configuration, excluding much ordinary application infrastructure unless explicitly supplied.

questions.question: What does @DataJpaTest fail to prove by itself?
questions.answer: That the production database dialect, migrations, networking and every transaction workflow behave identically to its configured test environment.

questions.question: Why can a @SpringBootTest pass without opening a real HTTP port?
questions.answer: Its selected web environment may use a mock context; choose a real server environment when the network boundary matters.

questions.question: How would you prevent test annotations from masking production wiring?
questions.answer: Assert selected integration identities and retain a small packaged-artifact smoke suite using production-like conditions and actual required infrastructure.
